messages.subject: featurecounts multi-map and multi-overlap modes
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I've run featurecounts (subread-1.4.5-p1-Linux-x86_64) using a bam file containing paired-end DNA reads mapped to an annotated bacterial genome.

Total fragments: 832927

Running ./featureCounts -T 6 -p -B -M -R -t CDS -g ID -a bact.gff -o s1_CDS_multimap.txt s1_sortcoord.bam produces

Assigned    714609
Unassigned_Ambiguity    97850
Unassigned_MultiMapping    0
Unassigned_NoFeatures    20468
Unassigned_Unmapped    0
Unassigned_MappingQuality    0
Unassigned_FragementLength    0
Unassigned_Chimera    0
Unassigned_Secondary    0
Unassigned_Nonjunction    0
Unassigned_Duplicate    0

and sum of counts in output txt file is : 714609

When I add -O option to the command above to also consider multi-overlaps, the count sum in the output file below does not match the total assigned.
 Is this correct? Are the counts inflated due to reads that may be overlapping more than one meta-feature?

Assigned    812459
Unassigned_Ambiguity    0
Unassigned_MultiMapping    0
Unassigned_NoFeatures    20468
Unassigned_Unmapped    0
Unassigned_MappingQuality    0
Unassigned_FragementLength    0
Unassigned_Chimera    0
Unassigned_Secondary    0
Unassigned_Nonjunction    0
Unassigned_Duplicate    0

Sum of counts in txt file 1,098,102

messages.subject: Re: featurecounts multi-map and multi-overlap modes
messages.body_plain:
Dear Camille Daniels,

Yes, this is expected. When you used the '-O' option, each read will be assigned to all their overlapping features and the resulting number of counts should be equal to or greater than the number of assigned reads. In your case, when you turned on '-O', you got 812459  reads that were successfully assigned but the total number of counts (1,098,102) is greater than the number of assigned reads since quite a few reads were counted multiple times.

In your first run of featureCounts summarization where '-O' was not used, 97850 reads were found to overlap with more than one gene and these reads were not assigned due to assignment ambiguity. 714609 reads were successfully assigned and each of these reads was assigned to only one gene. These reads plus the 97850 unassigned reads constitute the 812459  reads that were assigned in your second run where '-O' was turned on.

Hope this makes it clear.

Best regards,

Wei

messages.subject: New release 1.4.6
messages.body_plain:
Dear All,

We have made a new release of the Subread package. See the link below for details:

http://subread.sourceforge.net/

The Bioconductor R package Rsubread was updated accordingly as well. The latest version can be found at:

http://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/html/Rsubread.html

We are also delighted to report that our Subread-featureCounts-limma/voom pipeline was found to be one of the best-performing pipelines for the analyses of RNA-seq data by the SEQC/MAQC III Consortium. See the below paper published in Nat Biotech last month for the comparison results:

http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25150838

We have also created a new Bioconductor package called 'seqc', which includes the read count data and exon-junction data generated by using our pipeline. You can download this package from the following link:

http://bioconductor.org/packages/release/data/experiment/html/seqc.html   (188MB)

All the best,

Wei

messages.subject: Re: Soft-clipping of reads during mapping
Re: Soft-clipping of reads during mapping
messages.body_plain:
My apologies for missing this question.

Subread does soft-clip read bases. For your example, if the mis-matched base is the last base of the read, this base will be soft-clipped. If the mis-matched base is the second last base, no soft-clipping will be performed.

Subread performs soft-clipping by moving a 6bp window from the end of the read to the middle of read (to the region which is covered by the mapped subread). The window stops when both of the following two conditions are met:
(1) There are < 2 mis-matched bases existing in the window
(2) The last base of the window is a matched base.

After the window stops, all the bases after the window (between the last base of the window and the end of the read) will be soft-clipped. Subread does two rounds of soft-clipping: one from the 5' end of the read and the other from the 3' end of the read.

Soft-clipping makes the mapping output more accurate and it is useful for the downstream analyses. Why do you want to disable it?

Best wishes,
Wei

messages.subject: Re: Using Subjunc for Arabidopsis
messages.body_plain:
> <-n> Several libraries have very short reads (36 bp). When I aligned short-read library by TopHat, I often get high multiple alignment rates (offered by TopHat’s align summary). Since the read length of subheads is 16 bp, I wonder if I need to modify <-n> according to the read length.

If the default setting was used when you built the index (subread-buildindex command), subreads will be extracted from the reference genome in every three bases, ie. there is a 2-bp gap between each pair of neighbouring subreads. When using this index for alignment, you can only extract up to 7 subreads from a 36bp read ((36-15)/3). Subjunc by default tries to extract 14 subreads from each read. When there are less than 14 subreads available, it will extract as many as it can. For a 36bp read, it will extract 7 subreads which is the maximum number. So you do not need to modify -n. Subjunc takes into account the read length when it extracts subreads.

Another option you may try is to build a full index, ie subreads are extracted from every position of the reference genome. This will enable more subreads to be extracted for very short reads and it may further improve the mapping results. You can use the following command to build a full index:

subread-buildindex -F -B -f 72 -o subread_fullindex your_reference_genome.fasta

> Intron size. For Arabidopsis, the min/max intron size I tend to use is 50/2000. This would be very different from mammal genomes. So I wonder if  there’s a option for this.

We do not have a specific option for this. But I believe the current options should work well for your data. Subjunc requires the presence of donor and receptor sites when calling exon-exon junctions, so it should be pretty accurate for mapping your Arabidopsis data. It also favors shorter introns when a read can be best mapped to both a short intron and a long intron.

> Since the mismatch is not allowed for subhead, what does -M apply to?

-M is applied to the comparison between the entire read sequence and the target sequence. More specifically, it applies to the regions in a read which were not covered by the mapped subreads.

> <-d/-D> The meaning of these options changed in earlier version, so is the fragment/template length equivalent to mate inner distance? If not, is there an argument for that purpose?

-d/-D specifies the range of the lengths allowed for templates. It is not for the mate inner distance. You can actually set -d/-D values to get your required mate inner distance. For example, if your reads are 100bp long, you can set the minimum fragment length to be 250 to require the minimum mate inner distance to be 50.

./featureCounts -T 6 -t CDS -g ID -a bact.gff -o s1_trimmed_assembly_CDS_counts.txt s1_trimmed_assembly_sortcoord.bam

The following error is produced (also attached)

This bam file contains 875 reads.

I've re-run the file generation, both piping to samtools and running the sam to bam conversion separately), however they both generate the same error.

Can you help with resolving this issue?

Thanks in advance!
